question: What is the primary advantage of administering medication via the intravenous route?

options.B: Elimination of all potential adverse reactions
options.C: Bypassing the need for sterile equipment

explanation: Injecting fluids directly into a vein bypasses absorption barriers, delivering the substance immediately to systemic circulation. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: A patient requires rapid fluid resuscitation for severe dehydration. Why is the intravenous route selected over the oral route?

options.A: It avoids the cost of purchasing oral medications
options.B: It prevents the kidneys from filtering the fluids
options.C: It stimulates the digestive tract to absorb water
options.D: It restores circulating blood volume much faster

explanation: Intravenous infusion provides rapid volume expansion, which is critical in emergency dehydration and shock scenarios. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: Where should a nurse begin when selecting a peripheral vein for cannulation?

options.A: The most proximal sites near the shoulder joint
options.B: The large veins in the upper arm or shoulder
options.C: The internal jugular vein in the neck
options.D: The most distal sites on the upper extremities

explanation: Starting distally preserves higher venous sites on the same limb if complications arise and a new line is needed. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: Why is the antecubital fossa typically avoided for routine, long-term peripheral infusions?

options.A: Medications given there take too long to reach the heart
options.B: Arm bending can easily occlude or dislodge the cannula
options.C: Skin infections are completely unavoidable in elbow creases
options.D: The veins in this area have too many valves to pass a needle

explanation: Movement at the elbow joint creates mechanical stress that frequently kinks the catheter or irritates the vessel wall. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which intravenous fluid category expands the intravascular volume without causing major fluid shifts into cells?
explanation: Isotonic fluids share a similar osmolarity with blood plasma, keeping water balanced inside the blood vessels. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: A patient with cerebral edema requires a fluid that will draw excess water out of swollen brain cells. What type of fluid is indicated?
explanation: Hypertonic solutions create a higher concentration gradient in the blood, pulling fluid out of tissues and cells. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying a tourniquet prior to peripheral IV cannulation?

options.A: To engorge and make the superficial veins visible
options.B: To numb the skin area before needle insertion
options.C: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the limb
options.D: To sterilize the puncture site against bacteria

explanation: A tourniquet traps venous blood in the limb, filling the veins and making them easier to palpate and puncture. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: Which IV cannula gauge is most appropriate for a patient receiving rapid blood transfusion?
explanation: Larger bore needles with a smaller gauge number, like 18G, prevent hemolysis and allow viscous blood to flow rapidly. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: At what angle should a nurse typically insert a peripheral IV cannula into the skin?
explanation: A 15 to 30-degree angle allows the needle to pierce the skin and enter the superficial vein without puncturing through the back wall. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why is it necessary to let the skin antiseptic air dry completely before inserting the IV catheter?

options.A: To allow the chemical time to destroy microorganisms
options.B: To stop the vein from collapsing during needle entry
options.C: To prevent the antiseptic from stinging the patient's skin
options.D: To ensure the transparent dressing sticks to the area

explanation: Antiseptics like alcohol and chlorhexidine require adequate contact and drying time to achieve their maximal antimicrobial effect. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: What does a micro-drip infusion set typically deliver per milliliter of fluid?
explanation: Micro-drip sets always deliver 60 drops per milliliter, making them ideal for precise volume control in pediatrics. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: A nurse calculates an IV drop rate incorrectly, causing fluid to infuse far too quickly. What immediate risk does this pose?

options.A: Rapid crystallization of electrolytes in blood
options.B: Immediate collapse of all peripheral veins
options.C: Permanent numbness of the infused limb

explanation: Infusing fluids too rapidly overwhelms the cardiovascular system, leading to elevated blood pressure and fluid in the lungs. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: How often should a nurse routinely inspect a peripheral intravenous infusion site?

options.A: Whenever the intravenous fluid bag runs completely empty
options.B: During every nursing shift or per hospital policy
options.C: Only when the patient complains of sharp pain
options.D: Once every twenty-four hours during bed bath

explanation: Routine checks ensure early detection of localized complications like infiltration, phlebitis, or accidental dislodgement. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Why do nurses flush intermittent peripheral IV catheters with normal saline?

options.A: To cool down the internal lining of the vein
options.B: To stimulate local blood flow back to the heart
options.C: To dilute any medication previously given too fast
options.D: To clear residual blood and keep the lumen open

explanation: Saline flushes clear blood from the catheter tip, preventing clots from forming and occluding the cannula. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which sign is most characteristic of intravenous fluid infiltration into surrounding tissues?

options.A: Swelling and coolness around the insertion site
options.B: Severe itching across the entire chest wall
options.C: Bleeding around the transparent dressing tape
options.D: Hard red streaks tracking up the upper arm

explanation: When room-temperature IV fluid enters subcutaneous tissue instead of the vein, the area becomes swollen and cool to the touch. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: What is the priority nursing action when a nurse suspects phlebitis at a peripheral IV site?

options.A: Flush the line firmly with saline to clear the vessel
options.B: Administer a prescribed oral pain reliever for comfort
options.C: Stop the infusion and remove the cannula immediately
options.D: Slow down the infusion rate and apply an ice pack

explanation: Removing the catheter halts further irritation to the vein wall and prevents worsening inflammation or infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: What action should a nurse take immediately after withdrawing a peripheral IV cannula?

options.A: Apply a cold ice pack directly over the bare wound
options.B: Massage the puncture site vigorously to stimulate flow
options.C: Instruct the patient to bend the elbow joint tightly
options.D: Apply firm, continuous pressure to the site with gauze

explanation: Direct pressure prevents hematoma formation and stops bleeding from the puncture wound in the vein. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: Why is it important to pull the cannula out parallel to the skin surface during removal?

options.A: To prevent trauma and scraping of the internal vein wall
options.B: To ensure the plastic catheter tip does not break off
options.C: To allow the skin to close up faster without a bandage
options.D: To make sure the tape comes off without pulling hair

explanation: Withdrawing the cannula at the same low angle it entered prevents the tip from scraping or tearing the vessel lumen. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)
